text:
Can you write an email to people who didn't renew their farm share? I run a 30-acre vegetable farm and sell 22-week shares that people pick up every Thursday.

Facts:
- Last year 260 households had a share. 97 didn't renew.
- On July 9 a hailstorm destroyed about half our crops. For the next 6 weeks the boxes had about half the usual amount. We didn't offer refunds or credit, and I sent one short email about it.
- A full share is $540 this year, the same as last year.
- This year we've added a second field on higher ground and put up 2 hail nets over our tomatoes and peppers. That cost $31,000.
- Members can now pause up to 2 weeks and get credit for them.
- Sign-up closes March 15. 52 shares are left.

Under 200 words.

I have a few questions before I write this. The biggest thing these 97 households hold against you is that their boxes were half-size for six weeks, with no refund or credit and only one short email. Unless the email deals with that first, the improvements will read as a sales pitch.

1. **Do you want to apologize directly, and is there anything you can offer people who come back?** For example, a discount, a credit or a bonus box. Whatever you're willing to commit to will shape the email more than anything else. If the answer is nothing, I'll write the apology without an offer and won't hint at one.

2. **If a disaster cuts the boxes again, what happens now?** The hail nets only cover tomatoes and peppers, and the new pause credit is a different thing. People will want to know whether a short box would get credit next time. If you have a policy, or are willing to adopt one, that's what would win them back. If not, I won't suggest that you do.

3. **Do you know why people didn't renew?** Did any of them tell you it was the hail, or did some leave for other reasons, like moving or cost? This decides whether the whole email is about the hail or whether it's broader.

4. **How do people sign up?** I need the link or the steps.

5. **Who signs the email, and what's the farm called?**

1. Yes, I want to say sorry plainly. I didn't write more after the hail because I was working 16-hour days trying to save what was left. I'm not offering a discount or bonus box. But I can commit to a short email to members every Thursday of the season.

2. I can commit to a credit for any week when weather cuts a box by more than a third. I can't promise there won't be crop loss this year. And yes, the nets only cover tomatoes and peppers, not the greens.

3. 41 of the 97 answered a short survey in the fall. 29 of them said they'd come back if we fixed how we handle bad weeks.

4. Through the link on our website.

5. Sam Turner, Greenbank Farm.

I've drafted it below, at about 190 words including the subject line. It opens with the apology, before you ask anyone to come back.

- **The survey:** I wrote "many of you who answered our fall survey." That's accurate, since 29 of the 41 who answered said this. "Most of you" would not be, because that's only 29 of all 97.
- **Weather losses:** I said plainly that the nets don't cover the greens and that you can't promise there won't be crop loss. These readers would notice if the email skipped that.
- **The credit:** I didn't say "you'll get credit" for every bad week, because your policy only covers weeks when a box is cut by more than a third.

<final_document>
Subject: We got last summer wrong. Here's what's changed.

Hi,

I owe you an apology. After the July 9 hailstorm, your boxes were about half-size for six weeks. We didn't offer credit, and I sent one short email. I was working 16-hour days to save what was left, but I should have kept you informed. I'm sorry.

Many of you who answered our fall survey said you'd come back if we fixed how we handle bad weeks. So now:

- If weather cuts a box by more than a third, you get credit for that week.
- I'll send a short email to members every Thursday of the season, in good weeks and bad.
- You can pause up to two weeks and get credit for them.

We've also spent $31,000 on a second field on higher ground and hail nets over the tomatoes and peppers. The greens are still exposed, and I can't promise there won't be crop loss this year. But if it happens, you'll hear about it from me, not find out from your box.

A full share is still $540. There are 52 shares left, and sign-up closes March 15. You can join through the link on our website.

Sam Turner
Greenbank Farm
</final_document>
